question_text: What is the difference between CRR, SLR, and Repo Rate? How do they control money supply?
correct_answer: CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) is the percentage of total deposits banks must keep with RBI as cash — this money earns no interest. SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio) is the percentage banks must invest in government securities, gold, or approved securities before giving credit. Repo Rate is the rate at which RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities. Increasing these ratios reduces money in the system (contractionary), decreasing them injects liquidity (expansionary).
key_points: CRR: kept with RBI, no interest earned, currently ~4%
SLR: invested in govt securities/gold, currently ~18%
Repo Rate: overnight borrowing rate from RBI, key policy tool
MSF (Marginal Standing Facility): emergency overnight borrowing, higher than repo
tip: Always know current rates — CRR, SLR, Repo, Reverse Repo, MSF. Interviewers test current awareness.

question_text: Explain the structure of the Indian banking system and the role of RBI.
correct_answer: The Indian banking system is a two-tier system: RBI at the apex and commercial banks below. RBI functions: monetary policy (controls money supply), banker to government, banker's bank (lender of last resort), regulator and supervisor, foreign exchange management (FEMA), issuance of currency. Commercial banks: public sector (SBI, PNB), private sector (HDFC, ICICI), foreign banks, regional rural banks, small finance banks, payment banks. RBI has full control over monetary policy while government handles fiscal policy.
key_points: RBI: monetary authority, regulator, lender of last resort
Scheduled banks: SBI and nationalized banks, private, foreign
RRBs: rural banking promoted by central+state+sponsor bank
Payment banks: deposits only, no credit — Paytm, Airtel
tip: Know Basel III norms — RBI enforces capital adequacy requirements on Indian banks.

question_text: What is NABARD and what role does it play in Indian agriculture and rural development?
correct_answer: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) was established in 1982 following B. Sivaraman Committee recommendations. It is the apex development bank for agriculture, rural industries, and small enterprises. Functions: provides refinance to state cooperative banks, RRBs, land development banks. Supervises cooperative banks and RRBs. Runs RIDF (Rural Infrastructure Development Fund) for state government borrowings. Promotes SHG-Bank Linkage Programme — largest microfinance programme in the world.
key_points: Established 1982, apex body for rural/agricultural finance
Refinances state cooperative banks, RRBs, land development banks
RIDF: Rural Infrastructure Development Fund
SHG-Bank Linkage: largest microfinance program globally
tip: MUDRA Bank (2015) complements NABARD — NABARD for agriculture, MUDRA for micro-enterprises.

question_text: What are NPA (Non-Performing Assets) and how are they classified?
correct_answer: An NPA is a loan where interest or principal has been overdue for more than 90 days. Classification: Substandard (NPA for less than 12 months), Doubtful (substandard for 12+ months, full recovery questionable), Loss (identified by bank or auditors as uncollectable). Banks must provision (set aside capital) for NPAs: 15% for substandard, 25-100% for doubtful based on years, 100% for loss. Net NPA = Gross NPA minus provisions. SARFAESI Act 2002 enables banks to recover NPAs without court approval.
key_points: NPA: overdue 90+ days for term loans
Classification: Substandard (< 12 months), Doubtful, Loss
Provisioning requirements increase with worsening classification
SARFAESI Act: recovery without court for secured loans > ₹1 lakh
tip: Know gross vs net NPA and why banks want net NPA — it reflects the real loss after provisioning.

question_text: Explain the difference between NEFT, RTGS, and IMPS.
correct_answer: NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) is available 24/7, settled in batches of 30 minutes. No minimum/maximum limit. Best for non-urgent transfers. RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) settles individually in real time. Minimum ₹2 lakh, no maximum. Available 24/7. Best for high-value, time-critical transfers. IMPS (Immediate Payment Service) is instant, 24/7 including holidays. Limit up to ₹5 lakh typically. Best for urgent small amounts. UPI uses IMPS infrastructure for instant P2P/P2M.
key_points: NEFT: 24/7, batched (30 min), no minimum limit
RTGS: 24/7, real-time individual settlement, min ₹2 lakh
IMPS: instant, 24/7, up to ₹5 lakh
UPI: built on IMPS, VPA-based, via mobile app
tip: NEFT and RTGS moved to 24/7 in 2019 — interviewers may still expect you to note this change.

question_text: What is the SARFAESI Act and how does it help banks in NPA recovery?
correct_answer: SARFAESI (Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest) Act 2002 enables banks and financial institutions to recover NPAs without court intervention. Banks can: take possession of secured assets on 60 days notice, auction or sell the asset without filing a civil suit. Only applies to secured loans above ₹1 lakh. Borrower can appeal to Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT). Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) buy NPA portfolios from banks. CIBIL tracks the borrower's credit record.
key_points: No court needed for secured NPA recovery — 60 days notice
Minimum loan: ₹1 lakh, must be secured
DRT: borrower's appeal forum
ARCs like Edelweiss ARC buy NPA portfolios at discount
tip: IBC (Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016) works alongside SARFAESI for larger corporate NPA resolution.

question_text: What is financial inclusion and what are the key government schemes for it?
correct_answer: Financial inclusion means providing access to affordable financial services (bank accounts, credit, insurance, payments) to all sections of society — especially the unbanked rural and low-income population. Key schemes: Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) — zero-balance accounts with RuPay debit card and ₹2 lakh accident insurance. MUDRA: loans to micro-enterprises (Shishu, Kishor, Tarun). Stand-Up India: scheduled caste/tribe and women entrepreneurs. Atal Pension Yojana, PMJJBY (life insurance), PMSBY (accident insurance) as social security.
key_points: PMJDY: zero-balance account, RuPay card, overdraft facility
MUDRA: Shishu (up to ₹50K), Kishor (₹50K-5L), Tarun (₹5L-10L)
Stand-Up India: SC/ST and women, ₹10L-1Cr term loan
Business Correspondents (BC): banking agents in unbanked areas
tip: Know PMJDY numbers — over 50 crore accounts opened since 2014, largest financial inclusion drive globally.

question_text: Explain the concept of Basel III norms and their importance for Indian banks.
correct_answer: Basel III is a global regulatory framework from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision to strengthen banks' capital adequacy and resilience. Key requirements: Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) of minimum 10.5% (RBI requires 11.5% for Indian banks including CCB). Tier 1 capital (common equity) must be 6%, Tier 2 (supplementary) the rest. Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) ensures banks can survive a 30-day stress. Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) ensures long-term funding stability. Fully implemented in India by 2019.
key_points: CAR minimum 10.5% globally, 11.5% RBI mandate for India
Tier 1 (equity): 6%, Tier 2 (subordinated debt, provisions)
LCR: liquid assets to cover 30-day stress outflow
Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB): extra 2.5% on top of minimum
tip: In a banking interview, always connect Basel III to the 2008 financial crisis — it was designed in response to it.

question_text: What is the difference between commercial banking and investment banking?
correct_answer: Commercial banks take deposits from the public and lend to individuals and businesses — they make money on the spread between deposit rates and lending rates. They're regulated strictly by RBI. Investment banks assist corporations with raising capital (IPOs, bonds), mergers & acquisitions, and trading securities. They don't take retail deposits. In India, SEBI regulates investment banking activities. Universal banks (like SBI, HDFC) do both. Post-2008, Glass-Steagall-style separation discussions arose globally.
key_points: Commercial: deposits + loans, regulated by RBI
Investment: capital markets, M&A, IPOs, regulated by SEBI
Revenue: commercial from NIM (Net Interest Margin), investment from fees
India has universal banks doing both activities
tip: Know Net Interest Margin (NIM) = difference between interest income and interest expense as % of assets — key commercial bank profitability metric.

question_text: What is CIBIL and how does credit score affect banking?
correct_answer: CIBIL (Credit Information Bureau India Limited) is India's first credit information company. It collects credit information from banks and lenders and generates CIBIL scores ranging from 300-900. A score above 750 is considered good and qualifies for better loan terms and interest rates. Score depends on: repayment history (35%), credit utilization (30%), credit age, credit mix, and new credit inquiries. Banks check CIBIL before approving loans. CIBIL Report shows all active and closed credit accounts.
key_points: Score range: 300-900, 750+ is good
Repayment history: most important factor (35%)
Credit utilization: keep below 30% of credit limit
Hard inquiries from loan applications temporarily reduce score
tip: Four credit bureaus in India: CIBIL, Equifax, Experian, CRIF High Mark — though CIBIL is most used.

question_text: Explain Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) and how it sets interest rates in India.
correct_answer: The MPC is a six-member statutory committee constituted under RBI Act. Members: RBI Governor (chairman), Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer, and three external members appointed by the government. It meets at least four times a year (bi-monthly). Decisions by majority vote — Governor has casting vote in a tie. MPC sets repo rate to achieve inflation target of 4% (±2%) as mandated by Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework adopted in 2016.
key_points: 6 members: 3 RBI + 3 government appointed external
Governor chairs, casting vote in tie
Target: 4% CPI inflation ±2% band
Bi-monthly meetings — minutes released 14 days after
tip: India adopted inflation targeting in 2016 — before MPC, RBI had multiple objectives. Know this shift.

question_text: What are Priority Sector Lending (PSL) norms in India?
correct_answer: Priority Sector Lending norms require banks to lend a specified percentage of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to priority sectors. Domestic banks: 40% overall PSL target. Within that: 18% to agriculture (including 10% to small/marginal farmers), 7.5% to microenterprises, 10% to weaker sections. Foreign banks (with 20+ branches): 40% target. Shortfall is deposited in RIDF (NABARD) or SIDBI/NHB funds at lower interest. PSL certificates (PSLCs) allow trading of surplus PSL.
key_points: 40% of ANBC for domestic banks
Agriculture: 18%, Micro enterprises: 7.5%, Weaker sections: 10%
Shortfall deposited in RIDF at penalty rates
PSL Certificates (PSLCs): tradeable certificates for PSL compliance
tip: Foreign banks (<20 branches) have 8 target categories only, including export credit — know the differentiation.

question_text: What is the role of SEBI in regulating India's capital markets?
correct_answer: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) was established in 1988, given statutory powers in 1992. Regulates: stock exchanges (NSE, BSE), brokers, mutual funds, FIIs/FPIs, investment advisers, and depositories (NSDL, CDSL). Key functions: protect investors, promote securities market development, regulate market intermediaries. SEBI can penalize, ban, and prosecute violators. Recent initiatives: T+1 settlement, ASBA, ESG disclosures, direct mutual fund plans, algorithmic trading regulations.
key_points: Statutory body: Securities and Exchange Board of India Act 1992
Regulates exchanges, brokers, MFs, FPIs, advisers
ASBA: Application Supported by Blocked Amount for IPOs
T+1 settlement: India among fastest globally
tip: SEBI vs RBI jurisdiction: SEBI for securities markets, RBI for banking — corporate bonds regulated by both.

question_text: What is the difference between Demat and trading accounts and how does share settlement work?
correct_answer: A Demat (dematerialized) account holds shares and securities in electronic form — like a bank account for shares. Maintained by depositories: NSDL or CDSL. A trading account is used to buy/sell shares on the stock exchange. Broker provides a trading account linked to Demat and bank account. Settlement: Under T+1 (now standard in India), shares and funds are settled next business day. Shares transfer to Demat, funds to bank. SEBI mandates no debit of client funds beyond T+7 by brokers.
key_points: Demat: electronic securities holder at NSDL/CDSL
Trading account: used to place buy/sell orders on exchange
T+1 settlement: India's current standard (was T+2)
DP (Depository Participant): your broker as NSDL/CDSL agent
tip: Know the chain: Stock Exchange → Clearing Corporation (NSCCL/ICCL) → Depository (NSDL/CDSL) — shows process depth.

question_text: Explain the concept of inflation targeting and types of inflation in India.
correct_answer: India adopted Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) in 2016 with a 4% CPI target (±2%). CPI (Consumer Price Index) measures retail inflation based on basket of goods consumed by households — this is the primary target. WPI (Wholesale Price Index) measures prices at wholesale/production level — tracked but not the target. Core inflation excludes food and fuel (volatile). Food inflation is most impactful for India's poor and politically sensitive. RBI raises repo rate to cool inflation, lowers it to stimulate growth.
key_points: CPI is RBI's target — 4% ± 2% band
WPI: production prices, not primary target
Core inflation: CPI minus food and fuel
Food inflation most volatile — dependent on monsoon
tip: Know inflation categories: demand-pull (excess demand), cost-push (supply shortage), and stagflation (both high inflation and unemployment).
